title: Forget the judges: Maryland’s estate system is rigged against families
summary: A legislative task force studying the "efficiency, uniformity and quality" of Maryland's estate system needs to take a step back and look at the broader issue of a system designed to favor lawyers over families, writes J.H. Snider.
content:
by J.H. Snider, Maryland Matters December 27, 2025

by J.H. Snider, Maryland Matters December 27, 2025

A decades-long battle is raging between Maryland’s Orphans’ Court judges and the Maryland Bar Association over whether our probate judges should be lawyers or laypeople. The legislature recently threw down the gauntlet for the latest skirmish, passing legislation in its 2025 session to create a task force ostensibly to study “improving the efficiency, uniformity, and quality” of estate processes.

But this conflict is a sideshow. While the task force focuses narrowly on judges’ credentials, jurisdiction and elections, it is ignoring the fundamental problems harming Maryland families forced into the government’s labyrinthine estate system.

The Task force met eight times this fall and plans to meet again next spring and then issue a final set of recommendations before it adjourns June 30, 2026.

The stakes are enormous. More than 50,000 Marylanders die each year. The average estate costs between $30,000 and $60,000 to settle, draining assets through legal costs, executor compensation, and government fees. If litigation occurs, costs can easily skyrocket into the hundreds of thousands. Yet, this short-term economic waste pales in comparison to the family estrangement the system causes, inflicting damage that lasts for generations.

The professionals who profit from this system routinely blame families for the conflict. But this blame game sweeps under the rug their own role in fostering that conflict. The root problem is that lawyer interests are aligned with fiduciaries, not beneficiaries, because that is where they earn more than 90% of their fees.

Contrary to fiduciary rhetoric, the actual law incentivizes fiduciaries to act for their own benefit at the expense of less favored beneficiaries. If acted upon, these incentives cause family conflict because a family member is the fiduciary for most estates. While most family members value harmony, the estate process strongly incentivizes bringing existing family stress to a breaking point.

The current task force is a perfect example of this anti-family bias. Every single member of it is either a government official or a representative of the Maryland State Bar Association. There is an old saying in politics: If you aren’t at the table, you are the meal. In this task force, Maryland families are the meal.

The state of Maryland rakes in approximately $235 million annually in “death taxes” but spends only about 15% of that to administer the system. The rest subsidizes other state operations. Politicians remain torn between the fearful power of the lawyers’ trade association — magnified by the fact that roughly a quarter of legislators have law degrees — and a desire not to harm their constituents too blatantly.

If the Legislature genuinely wants to improve the system, it must pursue a “parasite-cleaning” reform agenda.

First, we must automate the disclosure of financial assets and transactions. This was a good idea when the Internet was invented in the 1990s, and it is an even better idea now. Professional fiduciaries continue to oppose this to protect their billable hours and evade accountability.

Second, we must empower AI to compete with licensed lawyers. The lawyers’ trade association has always fought competition, including the “unauthorized practice of law,” and their resistance to AI is no different. The government should mandate improved public access to estate case law and dockets so that AI models can train on this information and provide affordable legal services.

Third, we must require the elected registers of wills to actively educate families. The government currently allows the system to remain opaque; instead, it should mandate that registers educate families about deadlines, rights, and responsibilities. This information should be automated and customized, but it requires no AI — just a shift in priorities to support Maryland families rather than the donors who contribute to their reelection campaigns.

Finally, we must codify and simplify estate law. The current nonintuitive and complex estate law benefits lawyers more than Maryland families and results in widespread fiduciary practices that mock fiduciary ideals.

In 1853, Charles Dickens’ “Bleak House” famously observed, “The one great principle of English law is to make business for itself.” Sadly, in the subsequent 172 years, the estate process has become even more skewed against the interests of those it claims to serve.

While the various professional parasites feeding off the system glibly spout talk of championing the public interest, the number of families harmed by the system has increased by orders of magnitude. It is long past time for the legislature to place the interests of Maryland families first. A task force that actually champions families — rather than those who feed off them — would be a refreshing change.
